# On the targeting of voltage-gated calcium channels to neurotransmitter release sites

**Authors:** Morven Chin; Pascal S. Kaeser

**Affiliations:** Department of Neurobiology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

At the presynaptic active zone, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Cavs) mediate Ca2+ entry for neurotransmitter release. CaVs are a large family of proteins, and different subtypes have distinct localizations across somata, dendrites and axons. Here, we review how neurons establish and maintain a specific CaV repertoire at their active zones. We focus on molecular determinants for cargo assembly, presynaptic delivery and release site tethering, and we discuss recent work that has identified key roles of the CaV intracellular C-terminus. Finally, we evaluate how these mechanisms may differ between different types of neurons. Work on CaVs provides insight into the protein targeting pathways that help maintain neuronal polarity.

## Introduction

In a nerve terminal, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (CaVs) translate the action potential into Ca2+ entry for the triggering of neurotransmitter release. At conventional synapses, CaVs are concentrated at the active zone, a protein scaffold that forms secretory sites for synaptic vesicles at the presynaptic plasma membrane [1]. The spatial coupling of synaptic vesicles and the Ca2+ source enables rapid vesicle fusion that completes within milliseconds of action potential onset [2]. Specialized release sites within sensory cells and neuromodulatory neurons also exhibit robust, Ca2+-dependent neurotransmitter secretion, suggesting similarities in release site architecture [3,4]. Hence, effective neurotransmission requires that neurons establish and maintain a CaV repertoire at their release sites, a task with significant logistical challenges. CaV biosynthesis primarily occurs in the soma, and neurons need to transport CaVs to axonal release sites, which may be up to hundreds of millimeters away, and incorporate them into local release machineries (Fig 1). How neurons supply their axon with CaVs and prevent mistargeting to other compartments remains largely unanswered. In this review, we highlight recent advances on the interactions that tether CaVs to neurotransmitter release sites. We examine possible models for CaV axonal transport, and we discuss how these mechanisms may vary for different types of neurons.

## CaV genetics, subunits, structure and function

CaVs consist of a pore-forming CaVα1 subunit and in most cases auxiliary CaVβ and CaVα2δ subunits [5,6]. Vertebrates encode ten CaVα1 subtypes that are classified by their genetic and functional properties into CaV1s (CaV1.1-1.4, or L-type), CaV2s (CaV2.1-2.3, or P/Q-, N- and R-type, respectively), and CaV3s (CaV3.1-3.3, or T-type). CaVα1 subunits share a common membrane topology comprised of four homologous domains with six transmembrane segments each. The domains are interconnected by cytoplasmic linkers, and the first and last domains are flanked by intracellular N- and C-termini (Fig. 2a).

In most central neurons, the high voltage-activated CaV2.1s and CaV2.2s are the dominant channels at the presynaptic active zone where they support neurotransmitter release [7,8]. CaV2.3s are also present and contribute to plasticity [9]. CaV2s are well-conserved, and the C. elegans and D. melanogaster homologs UNC-2 and Cac, respectively, are important for synaptic exocytosis [10-13] (refs.10**;11**;12*). CaV1s localize primarily to the somatodendritic compartment for the regulation of gene transcription and excitability [14]. CaV1s also mediate neurotransmitter release at specialized sensory synapses and in axons of dopamine neurons [15-17]. CaV3s have a relatively low activation threshold and do not typically contribute to synaptic transmission, but they are modulators of neuronal firing [18].

CaV1s and CaV2s assemble into multi-subunit complexes with one each of four CaVβ (CaVβ1-4) and four CaVα2δ (CaVα2δ1-4) subunits that contribute to surface expression [6]. The mechanisms through which they facilitate CaV forward trafficking have not been resolved and may differ between CaVα1 subtypes. CaVβ, for example, may promote channel export from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by occluding an ER retention signal or may shield the channels from proteasomal degradation [19-21]. CaVα2δ interacts with the CaVα1 extracellular interface to regulate surface expression in heterologous cells and abundance in neurons [11,22,23] (ref.11**). However, the exact trafficking steps controlled by CaVα2δ have not been identified. They may occur early in CaV biosynthesis because perturbations of CaVα2δ occlude CaVs from neurites, and in nerve terminals, CaVα2δ may not be associated with CaVα1 and may have independent functions [8,23,24]. Importantly, CaVβ and CaVα2δ co-assemble with CaVα1 without bias for subtypes. CaVβ subunits are distributed across axonal and somatodendritic compartments [25], and CaVα2δ interacts with both CaV1s and CaV2s [22,23]. Finally, not all CaV2 axonal trafficking requires auxiliary subunits, and some targeting persists without them [10] (ref.10**). Taken together, the auxiliary subunits may regulate early trafficking checkpoints that are shared by axonal and somatodendritic CaVs but likely do not contribute to compartment-specific targeting.

Overall, CaVs exhibit diverse roles across cellular compartments. Given their similarities in structure and sequence, it is not apparent how neurons target specific subtypes to the presynaptic active zone. In principle, CaV2 specificity at the active zone could be achieved through selective sorting into the axon, or multiple CaVs may be trafficked into the axon, with only CaV2s selectively retained at the active zone. For either model, the underlying mechanisms should satisfy two points: 1) specific tethering interactions should recruit CaV2s to axonal release sites and stabilize them there; and 2) somatic CaV cargo assembly should enable access to the axon. We will discuss the current understanding of the mechanisms that target CaVs to nerve terminals in light of these two points.

## Determinants for tethering CaVs to neurotransmitter release sites

### The CaV C-terminus specifies compartment targeting

The CaV intracellular C-terminal tail is mostly disordered and accounts for 20-40% of the protein Apart from a short proximal stretch immediately following the last transmembrane segment and a few key sequence elements, C-terminal sequences are poorly conserved, even across CaVs that localize to the same compartment [8,22]. Recent work has established the C-terminus as a major determinant for CaV targeting (Fig. 2).

First, replacement of CaV2s in hippocampal neurons with a CaV2.1 that lacks its entire C-terminus depleted CaV2.1 from the active zone [8], and partial truncations of the distal C-terminus also led to localization defects at the Calyx of Held [26]. In hippocampal neurons, endogenous CaV1.3 is distributed somatodendritcally and is absent from axon terminals, and chimeric channels with the pore-forming sequences of CaV2.1 and the C-terminus of CaV1.3 were not targeted to the active zone [27] (ref.27**). Similarly, a chimeric CaV2.1 with the C-terminus of CaV2.3, a subtype with some presynaptic localization but limited roles in evoked release, failed to rescue CaV function at the Calyx of Held after knock-out of CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 [28] (ref.28*). Hence, CaV2.1 requires its endogenous C-terminal sequences for correct targeting and to support release.

Remarkably, the CaV2.1 C-terminus is also instructive for active zone targeting (Fig. 2b). Translocation of the CaV2.1 C-terminus onto the pore-forming part of CaV1.3 generated chimeric channels with robust active zone localization [27] (ref.27**). These channels restored synaptic transmission in CaV2 knockout neurons but retained CaV1 functional properties and blocker sensitivity. In summary, the CaV C-terminus has emerged as a key trafficking determinant. Sequences within the CaV2.1 C-terminus are together sufficient to specify CaV axonal transport and tethering at the active zone. Consequently, other CaV sequences must either be dispensable for presynaptic targeting or be redundant with C-terminal sequences.

### Active zone scaffolding sequences in the distal C-terminus

The active zone mediates rapid and efficient neurotransmitter release. Its chief functions include the docking and priming of synaptic vesicles, and the tethering of CaVs nearby (Fig. 3). Several protein families comprise the main components of the active zone: these are RIM, RIM-BP, Munc13, liprin-α, ELKS, and bassoon/piccolo [1]. Multiple CaV tethering interactions with these active zone proteins converge within the CaV distal C-terminus.

RIM-BP and RIM directly bind to a proline-rich sequence and a PDZ-binding motif in the CaV2 C-terminus, respectively (Fig. 2a) [29-31]. Together, RIM and RIM-BP tether CaVs to the active zone and control the coupling of CaVs to synaptic vesicles, as established through genetic experiments that delete RIMs and/or RIM-BPs and through mutations of the CaV2 C-terminal interaction sites [8,29,32-35] (ref.33**). Bassoon might further contribute to CaV targeting by binding to RIM-BP [36]. ELKS may also contribute, but its roles remain unclear. In mouse hippocampal neurons and at the C. elegans neuromuscular junction, channel numbers are not affected by ELKS deletions, but ELKS may control CaV2 function and subtype contributions at other synapses [33,37,38] (ref.33**). In whole, these interactions are important for CaV tethering because chimeric CaV1.3s with the distal active zone scaffolding motifs of CaV2.1 are localized to the active zone [27] (ref.27**).

Notably, single deletions of active zone proteins or of their respective interaction sites within the CaV C-terminus do not fully disrupt CaV active zone abundance, and in some cases have mild effects [8,26,29,32-34,36-38] (ref.33**). This resilience implies substantial redundancy in the mechanistic pathways for CaV tethering. Compound deletions of active zone proteins or of their interaction sequences produce stronger defects in CaV localization, but some CaVs persist in axon terminals even after these extreme perturbations [8,32-34,39,40] (refs.33**;40*). Hence, tethering is likely mediated by multiple parallel interactions. These interactions may be dynamic and organized into various sub-assemblies [1,31,41] (ref.41*). They may recruit CaVs to the active zone and stabilize them within the presynaptic release apparatus, and this might involve both known interactors and binding partners that are yet to be determined. In conclusion, active zone scaffolding motifs are major contributors to CaV2 localization, but they are unlikely the only determinants within the C-terminus important for targeting CaVs to release sites.

### EF hands and IQ motif in the proximal C-terminus

The CaV proximal C-terminus contains two EF hands and an IQ motif (Fig. 2a). The IQ motif binds calmodulin, and alongside the two EF hands, these structures have been implicated in Ca2+-dependent CaV modulation [42-44]. In recent work, the CaV2.1 proximal C-terminus, which contains the EF hands and IQ motif, was translocated onto CaV1.3. This resulted in a chimeric CaV1.3 channel with some presynaptic localization despite the lack of the CaV2 distal scaffolding motifs (Fig. 2b) [27] (ref.27**). Correspondingly, deletion of the first EF hand from the CaV2.1 proximal C-terminus abolished CaV2.1 active zone localization. These results established a role for the proximal C-terminus in CaV2 active zone delivery and indicated that the proximal sequences operate in concert with the distal motifs that tether CaV2s to release machinery.

The mechanisms of the EF hands in CaV trafficking are not understood. CaV EF hands may not bind Ca2+ but may support functions of calmodulin binding at the IQ motif [42,43]. Calmodulin, for example, regulates CaV1 surface clustering [45,46]. The first EF hand may support a similar trafficking interaction for CaV2s, but it remains unclear whether a calmodulin-dependent trafficking checkpoint can specify compartment sorting. Future studies should further probe the CaV proximal C-terminus for involvement in trafficking and clarify its mechanisms of action.

### Potential targeting mechanisms via intracellular loops or extracellular interactions

CaV2.1 and CaV2.2 bind to SNARE proteins via a synprint motif in the intracellular II-III linker, and peptide inhibition experiments suggested that these interactions control CaV2 positioning [47,48]. These early reports generated a promising model wherein SNARE proteins may recruit CaV2s and couple them to synaptic vesicle fusion. This model was challenged by later findings that the peptides that inhibited CaV2 targeting also impaired the targeting of channels without a synprint motif and that CaV2.2 splice variants lacking a majority of the motif retained axon targeting [49,50]. Furthermore, the C-terminus of CaV2.1 suffices to target CaV1.3, which does not have a synprint motif, to release sites [27] (ref.27**). Hence, the synprint motif is not the primary determinant of CaV2 active zone targeting.

Synaptic vesicle exocytosis is aligned to postsynaptic receptors [51]. Scaffolding material within the synaptic cleft interacts with both compartments to control this transsynaptic organization, and these interactions may also recruit and tether CaVs to the active zone. Neurexins are presynaptic cell adhesion proteins that contribute to CaV2 targeting, and neurexin triple knockout reduces presynaptic CaV abundance [52,53]. The mechanism of action has yet to be fully defined, and it might include CaV2 tethering through CaVα2δ [53,54]. CaV2s may also form scaffolding complexes with the synaptic cleft protein laminin-β2. Disruption of the laminin-β2 interaction with the CaV2 extracellular interface inhibits CaV2.1 clustering and impairs the maintenance and development of functional active zones [55,56]. Altogether, extracellular tethering interactions may contribute to presynaptic CaV2 localization, but they are likely not sufficient to mediate it and may not be CaV subtype specific.

## Axonal transport of voltage-gated calcium channels

How CaVs navigate the trafficking junctures prior to their tethering at the active zone remains an open question. CaV2s leaving the ER-to-Golgi biosynthetic pathway should be packaged into transport vesicles that must then pass through the axonal cargo filters, traverse the axon arbor, and be captured in nerve terminals before their CaV2 cargoes are incorporated into the release machinery (Fig. 1). As discussed above, the CaV2.1 C-terminus may instruct the assembly of CaVs into axonal transport vesicles. Trafficking determinants within the CaV2.1 C-terminus may do so by interacting with cytoskeletal motors, adaptor proteins or co-transported cargoes.

Given the extensive interactions of the CaV2.1 C-terminus with active zone proteins, one possibility is that CaVs and active zone proteins are trafficked together. Initial characterization of the axonal trafficking of active zone material identified cargo carriers that may co-transport much of the needed secretory apparatus. In this model, vesicles derived from the Golgi may carry piccolo and bassoon, as well as RIM and ELKS2 [57-59]. Immuno-isolation and analyses of these vesicles yielded evidence that CaV2s may also be present as a cargo [58].

Recent work, however, suggests that the trafficking of CaVs and active zone proteins is more complex than through transport by a unitary precursor vesicle. Brp and Cac, the D. melanogaster homologs of ELKS and CaV2, accumulate at distinct rates and developmental time-points at the larval neuromuscular junction [11] (ref.11**). Furthermore, active zone formation and presynaptic morphology remain intact when CaV2s are ablated [8,11] (ref.11**). Conversely, strong active zone perturbations only partially disrupt CaV2 localization [32-34,39,40] (refs.33**;40*). Finally, deletion of the cytoskeletal motor KIF1A or of its adaptor Arl8 selectively inhibits the delivery of synaptic vesicles and active zone material to axon terminals, but CaV2.1 abundance was unaffected [60,61] (ref.60*). Altogether, it is likely that the active zone is assembled in a step-wise fashion. ELKS1, for example, may arrive early to capture later-arriving cargo [62,63].

How might the CaV2.1 C-terminus instruct axonal transport if not by mediating co-transport with active zone proteins? A conserved binding site for the cargo adaptor protein AP-1 was identified in the proximal EF hand of CaV2.2. Mutagenesis of this site produced deficits in CaV2.2 delivery to distal neurites of dorsal root ganglion neurons and inhibited CaV2.2 surface trafficking in heterologous cells [64], raising the model that the CaV2 proximal C-terminus nucleates the assembly of axon-bound transport vesicles via AP-1. However, dorsal root ganglion neurons do not exhibit a typical axon-dendrite division, and AP-1 is also an adaptor for somatodendritic cargo [65,66]. Ultimately, mechanisms of the CaV2.1 C-terminus in axonal targeting remain to be determined.

## Specialized secretory systems and their CaV dependence

Not all neurons fully rely on CaV2s for neurotransmitter release. Specialized sensory cells and some neuromodulatory neurons use other channels at their release sites, which raises the possibility that CaV trafficking is differentially regulated in these cell types (Fig. 3b).

Retinal photoreceptors and auditory hair cells release neurotransmitter in response to sensory stimuli and they support high volumes of tonic vesicle fusion [3]. Their release machinery is arranged at plasma membrane-adjacent ribbons that tether synaptic vesicles and feed them towards the ribbon base where CaVs are anchored for Ca2+-triggering of exocytosis. Here, CaV1.3 or CaV1.4 are the dominant channels, and in contrast to CaV2s at conventional synapses, they support the structure of this specialized synapse [15,17,67,68]. While the ribbon itself is composed of Ribeye, a protein specific to it [69,70], the release site scaffolds underneath the ribbon bear striking similarities to active zones at conventional synapses. RIM, RIM-BP and bassoon play central roles in organizing release and CaV1s [71-74]. A key feature of these sensory cells is that they do not have a classical axon; instead, release is either from the soma or from a short neurite. The CaV1-dependence of the release machinery might in part be explained by direct interactions between CaV1s and RIM-BP [30,74] and by the absence of axonal trafficking filters.

Monoaminergic systems project throughout the brain to modulate synaptic circuits. These modulatory axons often do not form synapses, but instead release transmitter from varicosities into the extracellular space for volume transmission [4]. The release is action potential- and Ca2+-dependent, and CaV2-dependence has been described for many monoaminergic transmitters, but the low spatiotemporal resolution of the release measurements in early studies did not establish that these channels directly trigger release [4]. Striatal dopaminergic axons, for example, are under direct regulation of cholinergic axons. Experiments using CaV2 blockers over-estimated the roles of CaV2s in dopamine axons because these blockers also inhibited acetylcholine release, which in turn prevented cholinergic triggering of dopamine release [75,76]. When dopamine axons were optogenetically stimulated, or when CaV2s were selectively ablated in dopamine neurons, it was found that other channels robustly contribute to release, and both CaV1s and CaV3s may be part of the axonal CaV repertoire that triggers dopamine release [16,77].

For these neuromodulatory systems, many questions remain unanswered. First, while dopamine release strongly depends on the active zone proteins RIM and Munc13, these proteins are only present in a subset of varicosities, and many varicosities may not release dopamine in response to stimulation [78-80]. In contrast, Ca2+ entry appears to be present in most varicosities [80]. The distribution of axonal CaVs in neuromodulatory neurons is not known, and their spatial relationship to active zone proteins remains unclear. RIM domains that bind to CaV2s are important for neurotransmitter release at conventional synapses, but in dopaminergic neurons, they may be dispensable [29,79]. Future work should probe the distribution of CaV subtypes in dopamine axons and test whether active zone scaffolds are needed for their localization. Similarly, it is unclear how channels that are typically retained somatodendritically access the axon in dopaminergic neurons. Finally, the exact CaV repertoires that gate neurotransmitter release in other monoaminergic neurons remain to be defined.

## Conclusions and outlook

Effective trafficking and targeting of CaVs to neurotransmitter release sites is essential for brain function. Recent work has established the CaV C-terminus as a molecular determinant for CaV compartment targeting. However, major questions remain. How do the CaV C-terminal sequences permit axonal transport of CaV cargoes? Is the cargo carrier shared with other presynaptic proteins or are CaVs transported on their own? Which CaVs trigger release in neuromodulatory neurons? In dopaminergic neurons, how do CaV1 and CaV3 channels pass through the axonal sorting pathways? In summary, while past work has produced significant insight into the interactions that tether CaV2s at the active zone, further work is required to elucidate the mechanisms for CaV transport into axons and for tethering channels other than CaV2s at axonal release sites.
